answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type for a cluster/account: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (resource name is the Cosmos DB account).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the built-in core CLI group az cosmosdb. Example to create an account: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRg --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=westus2. (az cosmosdb is part of the core az command set, not a separate extension.)

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (example resource declaration: resource cosmos 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' = { name: 'myAccount' ... } ). Terraform (AzureRM provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_account (resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" { name = "myAccount" ... kind = "MongoDB" }).

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Typical CosmosDB (Mongo API) connection string: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retrywrites=false. Use TLS/SSL (ssl=true or tls=true), login as the MongoDB user, host suffix is *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com and port is 10255 (standard for Cosmos Mongo over TLS). SRV strings are generally not supported; use the explicit host:port string.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Capacity is billed in Request Units (RU/s) for provisioned throughput (manual or autoscale RU), and Cosmos DB also offers a serverless option (pay-per-request) in supported regions. There is not a vCore-based billing model for the classic Cosmos DB (Mongo API) account — you choose provisioned RU/s or serverless.

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: For the MongoDB API you authenticate with MongoDB-style credentials (database users created on the Cosmos account) using SCRAM (username/password) via the connection string. Cosmos DB management operations use Azure RBAC/Entra ID. Native Entra ID integrated auth for the Mongo data plane is not generally available for older Mongo API versions — drivers authenticate with the DB username/password in the connection string. (Management/ARM uses Azure AD.)

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers (for Node.js use the official mongodb npm package or mongoose on top). There is no Cosmos-data-plane-specific driver for Mongo API — you use the upstream MongoDB client. For management you use the Azure SDK (azure-mgmt-cosmosdb / @azure/arm-cosmosdb).

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: Historically Cosmos DB's Mongo API did not provide specialized "vector index" types; vector search is typically done by integrating with Azure Cognitive Search or external vector engines. Therefore there is no standard built-in create-index command for DiskANN/HNSW/IVF on Cosmos Mongo API. (If a managed variant exposed vector indexes, you would expect a createIndex call like db.coll.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { algorithm: 'hnsw', dims: 1536 }), but that is not a standard Cosmos Mongo API feature.)

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Use Azure Cognitive Search for full-text or hybrid search scenarios (index documents from Cosmos DB into Azure Search). Alternatively, MongoDB API supports MongoDB text indexes (db.collection.createIndex({field: 'text'})) if the API version supports it, but for richer/full-featured text + vector hybrid search integrate Cosmos DB with Azure Cognitive Search or an external vector search engine.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB's Mongo API implements specific MongoDB wire protocol versions corresponding to supported API versions (historically 3.2/3.6/4.0/4.2 at different times). Many Cosmos accounts expose compatibility levels (Mongo 3.6/4.0/4.2). Some MongoDB features are not supported or are implemented differently: server-side JavaScript, some admin commands, certain aggregation pipeline stages/operators, and earlier lack of full support for change streams; multi-document transactions were introduced only in later supported API versions. Expect gaps compared with a native MongoDB server.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is a Cosmos DB emulator for some APIs (SQL/Gremlin/Table/Cassandra) but official local support for the MongoDB API has historically been limited. For development I would run the official MongoDB Docker image (e.g. docker run -p 27017:27017 --name mongo -d mongo:latest) and test against localhost:27017. For verifying against the managed cluster use the live cluster; do not rely on full parity with emulator.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB's Mongo API historically did not support MongoDB change streams; instead use Cosmos DB Change Feed for change notifications on documents. Change Feed is available on containers and needs to be consumed with the Change Feed processor or Azure Functions binding; you don't enable change feed per document but it is available on collections/containers (and billed by RU). If newer Mongo API versions support change streams, they are not guaranteed for all compatibility levels.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Management/control-plane tooling for Cosmos DB is part of Azure's general management plane. For data-plane agent tooling you would use a service-specific MCP (if provided). In the absence of a dedicated MCP, the general Azure MCP server (with a CosmosDB/documentdb plugin) would be used. (I am not certain of the exact MCP product name or whether a dedicated 'documentdb' MCP exists in your environment.)

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Microsoft's original hosted JSON DB service was called DocumentDB; it evolved into Azure Cosmos DB (DocumentDB was the earlier name/SDK). Azure Cosmos DB is the current multi-model service; the name DocumentDB refers historically to the precursor. This DocumentDB/Cosmos DB is a Microsoft product and is unrelated to any independently maintained open-source project named "DocumentDB" (if such exists).

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB uses a proprietary Microsoft engine and storage system and implements the MongoDB wire protocol on top of it for Mongo API accounts. This means application code using standard MongoDB drivers generally works, but some server-side behaviors, admin commands, and performance characteristics differ (e.g. RU billing, some unsupported Mongo features). Expect small compatibility gaps; use standard drivers and test queries against the target account.

answers.question: Which database and collection names will this sample use?
answers.answer: Database: sample_banking_07. Collections: applications (primary collection for mortgage applications), agents (optional metadata about agents), decisions (or store decision status inside applications as a field). The sample will create/operate only in sample_banking_07.

answers.question: What index definition does this sample need for vector search (embedding field)?
answers.answer: Assuming the cluster supports vector indexes (as the run environment claims), create an index on the embedding field. Example (Mongo-style speculative): db.applications.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'embedding_vector_idx', algorithm: 'hnsw', dims: 1536, metric: 'cosine' }). If the service doesn't accept that, the fallback is to store embeddings and use an external vector search (Azure Cognitive Search or a separate vector service).

answers.question: How will the sample read the cluster connection details at runtime?
answers.answer: Read the connection string from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI in Node.js: const uri = process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI; then pass that to MongoClient (mongodb package). Example connector code: const client = new MongoClient(uri, { tls: true, useUnifiedTopology: true }); await client.connect();

answers.question: What TLS/port/connection options will the Node.js app enforce when connecting?
answers.answer: Connect to the managed cluster on port 10255 with TLS enabled and replicaSet globaldb. Example connection options appended to the URI: ?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retrywrites=false (or tls=true in newer drivers). The app will enforce TLS (rejectUnauthorized default) and use the provided credentials in DOCUMENTDB_URI.

answers.question: Which Node.js client library and version will the sample use to interact with DocumentDB's Mongo API?
answers.answer: Use the official mongodb npm package (Node.js driver) — target a recent major version (mongodb@5.x or 4.x depending on Node support). Use MongoClient from 'mongodb' to connect and perform CRUD and createIndex operations.
